title: Given a `List<Employee>`, produce a `Map<String, Long>` giving the number of employees in each department, using `Collectors.groupingBy` with a `Collectors.counting()` downstream.
shortTitle: Group employees by department, then count employees in each department into Map<String, Long>

s1_definition.profdef: The two-argument `groupingBy(classifier, downstream)` lets you replace the default list collector with another collector applied to each group. Passing `Collectors.counting()` as the downstream counts the elements per group, yielding a `Map<String, Long>` of department to head count.
s1_definition.analogy: Instead of keeping a tray of cards per department, Priya only wants a tally: how many people are in each department. So for each department she keeps a counter and ticks it up for every card. At the end she has "IT: 2, Finance: 2, HR: 1". The counting downstream is that per-department tally.
s1_definition.oneliner: `groupingBy(dept, counting())` gives the head count per department as a Map<String, Long>.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The two-argument `groupingBy(classifier, downstream)` lets you replace the default list collector with another collector applied to each group. Passing `Collectors.counting()` as the downstream counts the elements per group, yielding a `Map<String, Long>` of department to head count.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Instead of keeping a tray of cards per department, Priya only wants a tally: how many people are in each department. So for each department she keeps a counter and ticks it up for every card. At the end she has "IT: 2, Finance: 2, HR: 1". The counting downstream is that per-department tally.

**One line to remember:** `groupingBy(dept, counting())` gives the head count per department as a Map<String, Long>.

sections.s2_technical:
`Collectors.groupingBy` with two arguments takes the classifier and a downstream collector. The downstream is applied to the elements that fall into each group rather than collecting them into a list. `Collectors.counting()` is a collector that counts its inputs and returns a `Long`, so each group's value becomes the number of employees in it.

The result type is `Map<String, Long>` because counting produces a `Long`. For example, if two employees are in IT the entry is "IT" mapped to 2L. This is far more memory-efficient than grouping into lists and then calling size, because the elements are never materialised into per-group lists at all — only the counts are kept.

A senior point: the same result could be built with `Collectors.toMap(Employee::getDepartment, e -> 1L, Long::sum)`, but `groupingBy` with `counting()` is clearer and expresses intent directly. If I wanted sorted keys I would add `TreeMap::new` as the middle argument: `groupingBy(classifier, TreeMap::new, counting())`.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India's HR dashboard shows a head count per department for capacity planning. Grouping everyone into lists and then measuring each list wastes memory when all they want is the number. This is exactly how the counting downstream works — it keeps only a tally per department, never the full lists.

Problem 2 — The dashboard needs the departments in a stable order. This is exactly why the TreeMap factory matters — it keys the counts alphabetically.

The code defines `Employee`, a `HeadcountService` with `countByDepartment`, and a demo.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: Rajesh IT, Priya Finance, Amit IT, Sneha Finance, Vikram HR.

Step 1: Rajesh classified as IT; the IT counter becomes 1.

Step 2: Priya classified as Finance; Finance counter becomes 1.

Step 3: Amit classified as IT; IT counter becomes 2.

Step 4: Sneha makes Finance 2; Vikram makes HR 1.

Step 5: The TreeMap yields alphabetical keys with their counts.

```
INFO: Finance -> 2
INFO: HR -> 1
INFO: IT -> 2
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: [Rajesh/IT, Priya/Finance, Amit/IT, Sneha/Finance, Vikram/HR]
    │ collect(groupingBy(dept, TreeMap, counting()))
    ▼
  per-department tally (no lists kept)
    ├─ IT      → 1 → 2
    ├─ Finance → 1 → 2
    └─ HR      → 1
    ▼
  TreeMap<String,Long>
    ▼
  Output: {Finance:2, HR:1, IT:2}
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
To count employees per department I use the two-argument `groupingBy` with `Collectors.counting()` as the downstream collector. The classifier is the department, and instead of collecting each group into a list, the counting downstream tallies how many employees fall into each group, producing a Map from department name to a Long head count.

The efficiency point I always make is that this never materialises the per-department lists at all; it only keeps a running count per group, so it uses far less memory than grouping into lists and then calling size on each one.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India this fed an HR capacity-planning dashboard showing head count per department. I used a TreeMap factory so the departments came out in a stable alphabetical order. I also mention that the same numbers could be produced with `toMap(getDepartment, e -> 1L, Long::sum)`, but groupingBy with counting expresses the intent much more clearly, which is what I prefer for readable code.
